questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.series: Original AQA-style Group 2 and Group 7 Theory and Ion Test Interpretation
questions.question: Explain the opposing solubility trends for Group 2 compounds
questions.subtopic: AS inorganic structure, equations, trends, identification and RP4 observation reasoning
questions.prompt: Compare magnesium and barium hydroxides and sulfates. State how the solubility of each series changes from Mg to Ba and name the least soluble compound in each pair. Give one specified use for each of magnesium hydroxide and barium sulfate. [6 marks]
markPoints: Hydroxide solubility increases down Group 2.
Magnesium hydroxide is less soluble than barium hydroxide (Mg(OH)₂ sparingly soluble).
Sulfate solubility decreases down Group 2.
Barium sulfate is the less soluble sulfate (essentially insoluble).
Magnesium hydroxide can neutralise stomach acid as an antacid.
Barium sulfate is an X-ray contrast material; its very low water solubility is important.
questions.modelAnswer: For Mg–Ba, solubility of M(OH)₂ increases down the group. Mg(OH)₂ is sparingly soluble and is used as an antacid. Sulfate solubility decreases down the group: BaSO₄ is effectively insoluble and is used in medicine as an X-ray contrast material.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.series: Original AQA-style Group 2 and Group 7 Theory and Ion Test Interpretation
questions.question: Group 2 reactivity, electronic structure and water equations
questions.subtopic: AS inorganic structure, equations, trends, identification and RP4 observation reasoning
questions.prompt: Magnesium reacts much more slowly with cold water than barium. Explain the general change in Group 2 reactivity down the group in terms of shielding and ionisation energy. Give a balanced equation for barium reacting with water and state the gas formed. [6 marks]
markPoints: Group 2 metal reactivity towards water generally increases down the group (Mg to Ba).
Atomic radius and outer-electron distance from the nucleus increase down the group.
Electron shielding increases down the group.
Overall attraction for the outer electrons weakens and first/second ionisation energies generally decrease, so electron loss is easier.
Balanced equation Ba + 2H₂O → Ba(OH)₂ + H₂.
Identifies hydrogen gas and hydroxide formation.
questions.modelAnswer: Reactivity of Group 2 metals towards water increases from Mg to Ba. More inner electron shells mean greater shielding and greater distance to the two outer electrons. The attraction decreases, so removing the electrons is easier and ionisation energies are generally lower. Ba + 2H₂O → Ba(OH)₂ + H₂. Hydrogen gas is produced.

questions.question: Interpret a sulfate result and carbonate interference
questions.subtopic: AS inorganic structure, equations, trends, identification and RP4 observation reasoning
questions.prompt: A student reports a white precipitate when aqueous barium chloride reacts with an unknown aqueous sample. Explain why this alone does not prove sulfate is present; explain the purpose of the acidification stated in the AQA sulfate test. Write the ionic equation for barium sulfate formation and state one reason barium sulfate is suitable for use as a medical contrast material. [6 marks]
markPoints: Recognises sulfate ions as one possible explanation for the white precipitate.
Identifies carbonate ions as a possible alternative cause via barium carbonate precipitation.
Explains that acidification removes carbonate interference before sulfate interpretation.
States that Ba²⁺ reacts with SO₄²⁻ to form BaSO₄(s).
Gives a correctly balanced ionic equation Ba²⁺(aq)+SO₄²⁻(aq)→BaSO₄(s).
States that BaSO₄ has extremely low aqueous solubility, limiting dissolved barium-ion exposure.
questions.modelAnswer: A white precipitate with barium chloride may be BaSO₄, but BaCO₃ could also form if carbonate is present. Acidification removes carbonate ions and reduces a false-positive inference. The ionic equation is Ba²⁺(aq)+SO₄²⁻(aq)→BaSO₄(s). BaSO₄ is effectively insoluble, so very little dissolves in water.

questions.question: Identify three halides from precipitation and ammonia data
questions.subtopic: AS inorganic structure, equations, trends, identification and RP4 observation reasoning
questions.prompt: Three unknown samples were analysed by a school technician. In acidified silver nitrate tests, A gave a white precipitate, B a cream precipitate, and C a yellow precipitate. The precipitate from A dissolved in dilute aqueous ammonia; B dissolved only in concentrated aqueous ammonia; C remained insoluble in concentrated ammonia. Identify all three halide ions, give each silver halide formula, and explain why nitric acid, not hydrochloric acid, is used in the original halide test. [7 marks]
markPoints: Identifies A as Cl⁻ based on a white precipitate.
Names the precipitate from A as AgCl, soluble in dilute ammonia.
Identifies B as Br⁻ based on a cream precipitate.
Names the precipitate from B as AgBr, soluble only in concentrated ammonia.
Identifies C as I⁻ based on a yellow precipitate.
Names the precipitate from C as AgI, insoluble in concentrated ammonia.
Explains hydrochloric acid would introduce chloride and form interfering AgCl, whereas nitric acid does not introduce halide ions.
questions.modelAnswer: A is chloride, Cl⁻: white AgCl, which dissolves in dilute ammonia. B is bromide, Br⁻: cream AgBr, which dissolves in concentrated but not dilute ammonia. C is iodide, I⁻: yellow AgI, which does not dissolve in concentrated ammonia. Acidifying with hydrochloric acid would add Cl⁻ and produce a misleading AgCl precipitate, so the established halide test uses nitric acid.

questions.question: Halogen displacement and linked half equations
questions.subtopic: AS inorganic structure, equations, trends, identification and RP4 observation reasoning
questions.prompt: A student writes that aqueous chlorine can oxidise bromide ions to bromine, but aqueous bromine cannot oxidise chloride ions to chlorine. Give the balanced ionic equation for the first reaction, separate oxidation and reduction half-equations, and explain both predictions using the Group 7 oxidising trend. [6 marks]
markPoints: Gives full ionic equation Cl₂ + 2Br⁻ → 2Cl⁻ + Br₂.
Gives bromide oxidation half-equation 2Br⁻ → Br₂ + 2e⁻.
Gives chlorine reduction half-equation Cl₂ + 2e⁻ → 2Cl⁻.
Identifies chlorine as the oxidising agent (it accepts electrons).
States oxidising ability of halogens decreases down Group 7; chlorine is above bromine.
Explains bromine is too weak an oxidising agent to convert chloride ions into chlorine.
questions.modelAnswer: Cl₂+2Br⁻→2Cl⁻+Br₂. Oxidation: 2Br⁻→Br₂+2e⁻. Reduction: Cl₂+2e⁻→2Cl⁻. Cl₂ is reduced and is the oxidising agent. Oxidising strength decreases down Group 7, so chlorine oxidises Br⁻ but bromine does not oxidise Cl⁻.

questions.question: Relate halide reducing power to sulfur-containing products
questions.subtopic: AS inorganic structure, equations, trends, identification and RP4 observation reasoning
questions.prompt: In a theoretical comparison, solid sodium chloride, sodium bromide and sodium iodide each form an initial acid-base product with concentrated sulfuric acid. Further redox chemistry is observed for bromide and iodide, but not chloride. Explain the trend in halide reducing ability, identify the initial hydrogen halide formed from each salt, and name one sulfur-containing reduction product expected with bromide and one possible with iodide. Do not describe experimental methods. [6 marks]
markPoints: States halide reducing ability increases from Cl⁻ to Br⁻ to I⁻.
Explains larger, more shielded iodide ions lose an electron more readily than chloride ions.
Initial acid-base product for sodium chloride is HCl.
Initial acid-base product for sodium bromide is HBr and for sodium iodide is HI.
Bromide reduces sulfuric acid to sulfur dioxide, SO₂, with bromine formed.
Iodide can reduce sulfuric acid further, including formation of hydrogen sulfide H₂S (or sulfur S); iodine is formed.
questions.modelAnswer: Reducing power increases Cl⁻<Br⁻<I⁻ because outer electrons are more shielded and farther from the nucleus in larger halide ions. Acid-base reactions initially form HCl, HBr and HI respectively. Chloride does not significantly reduce the sulfuric acid. Bromide can form Br₂ and SO₂. Iodide is the strongest reducing agent and can produce I₂ with reduced sulfur products including elemental sulfur or H₂S. This is an equation/observation comparison only, not a practical procedure.

questions.question: Chlorine disproportionation in water and alkali
questions.subtopic: AS inorganic structure, equations, trends, identification and RP4 observation reasoning
questions.prompt: In the AQA Group 7 chemistry, chlorine produces both chloride ions and chlorate(I) ions when it reacts with water. (a) Write a balanced ionic equation for this reaction. (b) Assign chlorine oxidation states before and after. (c) Write the balanced equation for chlorine reacting with cold, dilute aqueous sodium hydroxide and name the compound providing chlorate(I) ions. (d) Name one benefit and one concern associated with chlorine used in water treatment. [8 marks]
markPoints: Water reaction balanced as Cl₂ + H₂O ⇌ Cl⁻ + ClO⁻ + 2H⁺ (or equivalent molecular equation Cl₂ + H₂O ⇌ HCl + HClO).
Initial chlorine oxidation state in Cl₂ is 0.
Final chlorine oxidation states are −1 (chloride) and +1 (chlorate(I)); recognises disproportionation.
Cold dilute sodium hydroxide reaction balanced as Cl₂ + 2NaOH → NaCl + NaClO + H₂O.
Names sodium chlorate(I), NaClO, as a product.
Explains it acts as a bleach/disinfectant because chlorate(I) compounds are oxidising agents.
Benefit: killing harmful microorganisms in treated drinking water.
Concern: chlorine toxicity or formation of potentially harmful chlorinated by-products, requiring careful control.
questions.modelAnswer: Chlorine with water: Cl₂+H₂O ⇌ Cl⁻+ClO⁻+2H⁺ (equivalent to Cl₂+H₂O ⇌ HCl+HClO). Chlorine changes oxidation state 0→−1 (Cl⁻) and 0→+1 (ClO⁻), so this is disproportionation. With cold dilute NaOH, Cl₂+2NaOH→NaCl+NaClO+H₂O. Sodium chlorate(I) is an oxidising bleaching/disinfecting component. Chlorine treatment kills harmful microbes, but chlorine and certain by-products pose health risks and require controlled levels.
